notes.summary: This chapter covers the SI system of base and derived units, significant figures and rounding off, dimensions of physical quantities, and dimensional analysis used to check equations, derive relations and convert units. CBSE tests it through one-mark MCQs on units and dimensional formulae, significant-figure arithmetic, and short derivations or unit conversions using dimensions.
keyPoints: Seven SI base quantities and units: length (metre, m), mass (kilogram, kg), time (second, s), electric current (ampere, A), thermodynamic temperature (kelvin, K), amount of substance (mole, mol) and luminous intensity (candela, cd). Plane angle is measured in radian (rad) and solid angle in steradian (sr); both are dimensionless.
Common prefixes: kilo 10³, mega 10⁶, giga 10⁹, milli 10⁻³, micro 10⁻⁶, nano 10⁻⁹, pico 10⁻¹², femto 10⁻¹⁵. Handy units: 1 Å = 10⁻¹⁰ m, 1 fermi = 10⁻¹⁵ m, 1 light year ≈ 9.46 × 10¹⁵ m.

Significant figures: all non-zero digits count; zeros between non-zero digits count; leading zeros never count (0.0025 has 2); trailing zeros after a decimal point count (4.700 has 4). Changing units does not change the number of significant figures (4.700 m = 470.0 cm).

Arithmetic rules: in multiplication or division keep as many significant figures as the least precise factor (2.5 × 1.25 = 3.1); in addition or subtraction keep as many decimal places as the term with the fewest decimal places (12.11 + 18.0 + 1.013 = 31.1).

Rounding off: if the dropped digit is more than 5, raise the previous digit; if less than 5, leave it; if it is exactly 5, leave the previous digit if it is even and raise it if it is odd (2.745 → 2.74, 2.735 → 2.74).

Must-know dimensional formulae: force [MLT⁻²]; work, energy and torque [ML²T⁻²]; power [ML²T⁻³]; pressure, stress and Young's modulus [ML⁻¹T⁻²]; momentum and impulse [MLT⁻¹]; Planck's constant and angular momentum [ML²T⁻¹]; G [M⁻¹L³T⁻²]; strain, angle and refractive index are dimensionless.

Principle of homogeneity: only quantities with the same dimensions can be added, subtracted or equated. So in (P + a/V²), a/V² has the dimensions of pressure, giving [a] = [ML⁵T⁻²]. Arguments of sin, log and exponential functions must be dimensionless.
Unit conversion: n₂ = n₁ [M₁/M₂]ᵃ [L₁/L₂]ᵇ [T₁/T₂]ᶜ for a quantity of dimensions [MᵃLᵇTᶜ]. Examples: 1 J = 10⁷ erg, 1 N = 10⁵ dyne, G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻² = 6.67 × 10⁻⁸ dyne cm² g⁻².

Deriving relations: assuming T ∝ lᵃ mᵇ gᶜ for a pendulum gives T = k√(l/g). Limitations: dimensional analysis cannot find dimensionless constants (k = 2π), cannot derive relations containing sums of terms or trigonometric/exponential functions, and a dimensionally correct equation is not necessarily physically correct.
traps: Counting leading zeros as significant, or forgetting that trailing zeros after a decimal point are significant.
Applying the significant-figure rule for multiplication to addition problems; addition is limited by decimal places, not by the number of significant figures.
Always rounding a final 5 upward, instead of keeping the preceding digit when it is even.
Converting squared or inverse units wrongly: 1 m² = 10⁴ cm² (not 10² cm²) and 1 kg⁻² = 10⁻⁶ g⁻².
Assuming that a dimensionally correct equation must be right; s = ut + at² is dimensionally correct but physically wrong.
notes.examTip: For any dimension question, first write the defining formula (F = ma, P = F/A, E = hν) and reduce it to M, L and T step by step instead of recalling the answer from memory.

questions.text: Which of the following is the SI unit of luminous intensity?
questions.explanation: Luminous intensity is one of the seven SI base quantities. Its base unit is the candela (cd). The lumen is the unit of luminous flux and the lux is the unit of illuminance; both are derived units. So the answer is candela.

questions.text: One nanometre (1 nm) is equal to:
questions.explanation: The SI prefix nano (n) stands for 10⁻⁹. So 1 nm = 10⁻⁹ m. For comparison, 10⁻⁶ m is a micrometre, 10⁻¹⁰ m is an angstrom (Å) and 10⁻¹² m is a picometre. Hence 1 nm = 10⁻⁹ m.

questions.text: The SI unit of plane angle is the:
questions.explanation: Plane angle dθ = arc length ds ÷ radius r, so it is a ratio of two lengths. Its SI unit is the radian (rad). The steradian (sr) is the SI unit of solid angle, while the degree and the revolution are not SI units. So the answer is radian.

questions.text: According to the rounding-off rules followed in NCERT, the number 2.745 rounded off to three significant figures is:
questions.explanation: The digit to be dropped is 5 with nothing after it. In this case the preceding digit is left unchanged if it is even and increased by 1 if it is odd. Here the preceding digit is 4, which is even, so it stays 4. Hence 2.745 rounds off to 2.74.

questions.text: Three masses, 12.11 g, 18.0 g and 1.013 g, are added together. The total mass, reported with the correct number of significant figures, is:
questions.explanation: Direct sum = 12.11 + 18.0 + 1.013 = 31.123 g. In addition or subtraction, the result keeps as many decimal places as the term with the fewest decimal places. 18.0 g has only one decimal place, so the sum is rounded to one decimal place. Total mass = 31.1 g.

questions.text: The length and breadth of a rectangular sheet are measured as 2.5 m and 1.25 m. Its area, expressed with the correct number of significant figures, is:
questions.explanation: Area = 2.5 m × 1.25 m = 3.125 m². In multiplication or division, the result keeps as many significant figures as the factor with the fewest significant figures. 2.5 has 2 significant figures (1.25 has 3), so the area is rounded to 2 significant figures. Area = 3.1 m².

questions.text: In the following equations, u and v are velocities, a is acceleration, t is time and s is displacement. Which equation is dimensionally INCORRECT?
questions.explanation: By the principle of homogeneity, every term of an equation must have the same dimensions. In s = ut² + ½at, the term ut² has dimensions [LT⁻¹][T²] = [LT] and the term at has [LT⁻²][T] = [LT⁻¹], while s has [L]. The terms do not match, so this equation is dimensionally incorrect. In each of the other three equations all terms have the same dimensions.

questions.text: The energy of a photon is given by E = hν, where ν is the frequency. The dimensional formula of Planck's constant h is:
questions.explanation: h = E/ν. Energy E has dimensions [ML²T⁻²] and frequency ν has dimensions [T⁻¹]. So [h] = [ML²T⁻²] ÷ [T⁻¹] = [ML²T⁻¹]. This is the same as the dimensional formula of angular momentum. Answer: [ML²T⁻¹].

questions.text: The time period T of a simple pendulum is assumed to depend on its length l, the mass m of the bob and the acceleration due to gravity g as T ∝ lᵃ mᵇ gᶜ. Using dimensional analysis, the values of a, b and c are:
questions.explanation: Write the dimensions: [T] = [L]ᵃ [M]ᵇ [LT⁻²]ᶜ = [Lᵃ⁺ᶜ Mᵇ T⁻²ᶜ]. Comparing powers of M: b = 0. Comparing powers of T: −2c = 1, so c = −½. Comparing powers of L: a + c = 0, so a = ½. Hence T = k√(l/g) with a = ½, b = 0, c = −½ (the constant k = 2π cannot be found from dimensions).

questions.text: The value of the universal gravitational constant in SI units is G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻². Its value in CGS units (dyne cm² g⁻²) is:
questions.explanation: Use 1 N = 10⁵ dyne, 1 m² = (10² cm)² = 10⁴ cm² and 1 kg⁻² = (10³ g)⁻² = 10⁻⁶ g⁻². So G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ × 10⁵ × 10⁴ × 10⁻⁶ dyne cm² g⁻². Adding the powers of ten: −11 + 5 + 4 − 6 = −8. G = 6.67 × 10⁻⁸ dyne cm² g⁻².

questions.text: In the van der Waals equation (P + a/V²)(V − b) = RT, P is pressure and V is volume. The dimensional formula of the constant a is:
questions.explanation: Only quantities with the same dimensions can be added, so a/V² must have the dimensions of pressure. Hence a = P × V². [P] = [ML⁻¹T⁻²] and [V²] = [L³]² = [L⁶]. So [a] = [ML⁻¹T⁻²][L⁶] = [ML⁵T⁻²]. (By the same rule, b has the dimensions of volume, [L³].)
